title: Calibrating a held-out-trial falsification rule
question: When one trial is withheld and its contrast predicted from the rest, which pass or fail rule holds its type I error, how much power does it have, and what does omitting a variance component or mis-targeting the prediction do?
design: One individual-data trial and five aggregate trials with a continuous outcome and linear effect modification; 24 cells crossing violation size, heterogeneity, covariate spread and withheld-trial position; full, naive, mis-targeted and decision-flip rules. 2000 replicates per cell.
answer: A held-out-trial check has a controllable size if the prediction targets the withheld trial's own population and its variance includes between-trial heterogeneity: the full rule's size was 0.035 to 0.073 (registered limit 0.07, exceeded by 0.003 in one scenario). Omitting heterogeneity raised size to 0.104, and aiming the prediction at the remaining trials' population raised it to 0.96. Power against a violation as large as the effect was only 0.21 to 0.47, so a pass licenses very little.
findings: Registered verdict: FULL RULE SIZE NOT HELD, by 0.003 in one of 8 null scenarios (MCSE 0.006); every other null scenario 0.035 to 0.064.
Power of the full rule: 0.07 to 0.17 at violation 0.15 and 0.21 to 0.47 at violation 0.3.
Null mean of the discrepancy: at most 0.009 with the external target, down to -0.60 with the reduced-network target.
Sign-disagreement rule: flagged 0.02 to 0.44 of valid analyses depending on the effect's distance from zero.
not_answered: Continuous outcome and G-computation only; no MAIC weight variance, no Bayesian predictive or conditional-moment rule; five aggregate trials. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: The withheld trial's contrast in its own population, and the discrepancy between prediction and observation
